newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Shell reports "significant" Kudu gas finds.
newsitem.headline: Shell reports "significant" Kudu gas finds.

text.p: Shell Exploration and Production Namibia BV on Tuesday reported that it had discovered "significant" gas reserves in its Kudu-4 field.
Managing director Ger Kegge said in a statement that it would, however, be some time before the full implications of the find could be spelt out.
Shell started drilling tests in the field on Monday to "provide essential information regarding the reservoir deliverability and gas quality".
"Kudu-4 encountered gas-bearing reservoir sands, confirming the presence of a significant energy resource in Namibian waters," Kegge said.
The test would take five days and together with the core and log information already gathered, the test data would be used in extensive follow up work to be included in an integrated field review.
"That study, scheduled for completion in the next six months, will provide critical support for appraisal and development planning.
"Scenarios being considered as part of this effort are a large volume export scheme to South Africa together with a fast track development to meet local energy demands within Namibia."

Kegge said initial results confirmed that the field extended to the south of earlier wells "but most importantly demonstrate that the sub-surface seismic model is capable of predicting the existence of porous reservoir sands."

This made it likely that there were additional possible reserves not highlighted by current 3D surveys and a new survey would start later this month next to the Kudu area and would probably increase reserve potential.

There has been considerable speculation lately about the exact size of the gas field, with estimates ranging from seven trillion cubic feet (tcf) to 14 tcf, which would make it a world class gas deposit.
But Kegge has repeatedly stressed that it is too early to make any meaningful assessment and that this week's tests would only start to provide a clearer picture.
"Full implications to reserves will only be available after completion of the appraisal/development planning study," Kegge said in the statement on Tuesday.

"It is already clear that the well has contributed significantly to the key objective of identifying economic gas reserve volumes sufficient to meet Namibian requirements and also support a large volume export scheme."
The latter was particularly important as it would allow the gas, which would compete against cheap South African coal, to be sold at competitive prices.
So far, there has been little enthusiasm on the South African side, although Minerals and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna recently pledged to help promote the use of gas in South Africa.

"Further appraisal drilling will, however, be required to confirm the gas reserves to the level of confidence which will enable commitment to the very significant expenditure needed to support such developments by the partnership," Kegge said.
Shell's partners in the scheme are Texaco Namibia Resources Inc and Energy Africa.
